Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Nobody is asked about their own phone. Say slowly that a student who already sent something is not in trouble and it isn’t too late. If a student is being threatened now, go with them to a counselor or administrator that day.

Every student in the room

Financial sextortion mostly targets teen boys, LGBTQ+ students can be targeted with threats to out them, and some students can't go to family first; every one of them should hear that school staff can help and they aren't in trouble.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can tell pressure from someone they know apart from a sextortion scam, recognize the scam script early, say no in words that sound like them, and know the exit if something they sent is being used against them: stop, save, block, tell. The message to land: it's never too late to get help, and the person being threatened is the victim.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 3 minBefore we start, and two different situations
  2. 5 minWho scammers target, and the script they follow
  3. 3 min“Everyone sends them”? About 3 in 20
  4. 7 minRead the pressure, and say your no: turn and talk, share out
  5. 12 minFour real situations, one per slide
  6. 5 minIf it already happened: stop, save, block, tell
  7. 10 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Two situations, the scam script, read the pressure, two of the four situations, and stop, save, block, tell.

Before you teach
Assume someone in the room has sent a photo.

Statistically, someone has, and someone may be under threat right now. Keep the tone free of blame: pressure and scams are someone else doing wrong. Never ask who has sent anything.

Talk directly to the boys.

Financial sextortion mostly targets teen boys 14 to 17. Many boys think this is a girls' issue. Say the numbers out loud.

If a student is being threatened.

Act the same day, ideally right away. Stay with them, tell them they aren't in trouble, and walk them to a counselor. Remind them not to pay or send more, and to save the messages before blocking.

Watch for hopelessness.

Students caught in a sextortion threat can feel there's no way out. If anyone says that, take it seriously and walk them to a counselor that day. 988 is there any time.

Be accurate about the law without scaring.

Images of anyone under 18 are illegal to create, ask for, keep or share, even with agreement. Also say that Massachusetts created a diversion program for teen sexting, and that a person being threatened is treated as the victim.

If a student mentions an image going around.

Don't ask for names in class. Afterward, connect the student with a counselor. Take It Down can help remove images of people under 18.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Boys as targets.

Boys are often ashamed to tell anyone and expect to be laughed at. Normalize telling: "This is a crime done to you, and adults help boys with this all the time."

LGBTQ+ students.

Scammers may threaten to out someone. Students who aren't out at home may feel they can't tell family. Make clear that a counselor or NCMEC can help without going through family first.

When home isn't the right place.

Some students live with relatives, foster parents or adults who would react harshly. "Tell an adult you trust" can mean a counselor, nurse or coach.

Faith and culture.

In some families, any sexual image would bring deep shame. That shame is what scammers use. Say plainly that the person being threatened did nothing that makes them deserve this.

Money.

Scammers ask for gift cards or payment apps. Students with little money may panic more. Paying almost never ends it, whatever someone can afford.

Language and immigration.

Students from immigrant families may fear police contact. NCMEC's CyberTipline and Take It Down are ways to report and remove images that don't start with police.

What the research says

From October 2021 to March 2023, the FBI and Homeland Security Investigations received more than 13,000 reports of financial sextortion of minors, involving at least 12,600 victims, mostly boys.

Federal Bureau of Investigation, 2024

From August 2022 to August 2023, NCMEC received an average of 812 sextortion reports a week, most financial and mostly involving boys 14 to 17.

Thorn and NCMEC, 2024

By 2025, NCMEC was receiving about 137 financial sextortion reports a day.

NCMEC CyberTipline data, 2025

Across 39 studies with more than 110,000 young people, about 15% had sent a sext and about 27% had received one.

Madigan et al., JAMA Pediatrics, 2018

In a survey of Massachusetts students, almost half of those who had sent a sexual image said it had been passed on without their consent.

Englander and McCoy, International Journal of Technoethics, 2017

Most college students who had sexted reported at least some pressure or coercion.

Englander, 2015

Massachusetts made sharing intimate images without consent a crime in 2024, including AI fakes, with a diversion program for teen sexting. The federal TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) requires covered platforms to remove reported images within 48 hours.

Mass. Acts 2024, c. 118; TAKE IT DOWN Act, 2025
